resources.string: How the rectus abdominis bends the trunk
Rectus abdominis and trunk flexion
A side view of normal spinal flexion with the pelvis held still. One of the two rectus muscles is shown at the front. Angles and shading are illustrative, not measurements.
Between ribs and pubis
The two rectus muscles lie on either side of the front midline. They run between the pubic crest and symphysis below and the xiphoid process and fifth to seventh costal cartilages above.
The front wall begins to shorten
Both sides of the rectus abdominis help start forward bending. With the pelvis still, the lower rib cage begins to move toward the pubis.
The trunk bends forward
As the spine bends, the rectus shortens along the inside of the curve and its tendinous intersections move closer together. The pelvis does not tilt in this example.
The rectus lengthens again
The rib cage moves away from the pubis as the trunk approaches neutral. Abdominal muscles can stay active as they lengthen to help control the return.
Back at neutral
The lower rib cage settles back over the same pelvis. The rectus returns to its starting length and the extra effort used to bend the trunk subsides.

Rectus abdominis, anterior view
The upper ends attach to the fifth to seventh costal cartilages and the xiphoid process of the sternum.
The two long rectus muscles run vertically on either side of the midline of the front abdominal wall.
Linea alba
This fibrous midline separates the left and right rectus muscles.
Tendinous intersection
Transverse bands of connective tissue divide the rectus into a series of muscle segments.
The lower ends attach to the pubic crest and pubic symphysis, at the front of the pelvis.
